---
title: "How to load encoding volumes"
---

This guide downloads and loads **encoding volumes** — a pre-computed 4-D volumetric
representation of electrophysiological features on the Allen Common Coordinate Framework
(CCF). Where the [channel features](load-channel-features.qmd) are a table of measured
channels, an encoding volume is the features projected onto a regular voxel grid covering
the whole brain.

::: {.callout-important}
These volumes are in a private S3 bucket and need an IBL account — pass a logged-in
`one.api.ONE` instance.
:::

## S3 layout

```text
aggregates/atlas/encoding_volumes/{project}/{label}/
├── brainwide_ephys_atlas_{res_um}um.npz   4-D volume (nx, ny, nz, N_features)
└── brainwide_ephys_edges_{res_um}um.npz   ephys edges (nx, ny, nz, 1), 2026_W39 onwards
```

Encoding volumes are versioned along **two** independent axes: the vintage label
(`label`) and the voxel resolution (`res_um`, in µm). A 25 µm volume is roughly
`(456, 528, 320)` and ~500 MB; a 50 µm volume is `(228, 264, 160)` — 138 MB for
`2026_W42`, which, like `2026_W39`, is published at 50 µm only.

Which vintages and resolutions exist changes as new ones are published. List them rather
than assuming:

```python
import ephysatlas.data

labels = ephysatlas.data.list_available_labels(one=one, project="ea_active")
```

## Download

```python
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from one.api import ONE
from ephysatlas.data import download_encoding_volume

one = ONE()
local_path = Path("/datadisk/ephys-atlas/volumes")

# res_um omitted -> auto-resolves to the finest resolution available for this label
file_path = download_encoding_volume(local_path, label="2026_W42", one=one)

# allow_pickle: older vintages store feature_names as an object array
data = np.load(file_path, allow_pickle=True)
```

`label` defaults to `"2026_W42"`. Pass `res_um` explicitly to pick a resolution when a
vintage has more than one, such as the 25 µm `2026_W12` volume:

```python
file_path = download_encoding_volume(
    local_path, label="2026_W12", res_um=25, one=one
)
```

## What the file contains

`N` is the number of features for that vintage: 41 for the `2026_W12` and `2026_W26`
volumes, 43 for `2026_W39` and `2026_W42`. From `2026_W39` the set has the spike-shape
columns (`spike_width_secs`, ...) instead of the raw waveform ones (`peak_val`, ...), and
adds `spatial_spread_um` and `slowness_s_per_m`. `2026_W42` names the first spatial
differences `*_bpr`.

| key | shape | dtype | description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ephys_atlas_vol` | `(nx, ny, nz, N)` | float16 | The 4-D volume: x × y × z × features, i.e. ML × AP × DV |
| `feature_names` | `(N,)` | str (object in older vintages) | Feature name strings, ordered as the last axis |
| `mean_per_feature` | `(N,)` | float32 | Per-feature normalisation mean |
| `std_per_feature` | `(N,)` | float32 | Per-feature normalisation standard deviation |
| `grid_shape` | `(3,)` | int32 | Volume grid dimensions `[nx, ny, nz]` |
| `res_um` | `(1,)` | int32 | Voxel resolution, µm |

## Extract one feature's volume

Always look the feature up by name — the ordering of the last axis is not guaranteed
stable across vintages:

```python
vol = data["ephys_atlas_vol"]
feature_names = data["feature_names"]

idx = np.where(feature_names == "rms_ap")[0][0]
rms_ap_volume = vol[..., idx]   # (nx, ny, nz) float16
```

The axis order is ML × AP × DV. `iblatlas` atlases use AP × ML × DV, so transpose the
first two axes (`np.transpose(vol, (1, 0, 2, 3))`) before indexing a volume with atlas
coordinates.

### Older volumes and the spike-shape columns

Volumes before `2026_W39` carry the raw waveform columns. To compare them with newer
tables, `remap_waveform_shape_features_volume` applies the same remap as the channel
tables:

```python
from ephysatlas.features import remap_waveform_shape_features_volume

shape_vol, shape_names = remap_waveform_shape_features_volume(vol, feature_names)
```

It returns only the 16 spike-shape channels (`ModelSpikeShapeFeatures` order), not the
whole volume. On a volume that is already remapped, such as `2026_W39`, the raw columns
are missing and it raises `KeyError`.

## Units and normalisation

Values are stored in **raw, unnormalised feature units**, with `0.0` outside the brain
mask.

`mean_per_feature` and `std_per_feature` are provided for optional z-scoring and are
**not** pre-applied. To z-score:

```python
z = (vol[..., idx] - data["mean_per_feature"][idx]) / data["std_per_feature"][idx]
```

::: {.callout-warning}
`0.0` outside the brain mask is indistinguishable from a genuine zero measurement. Build
a mask from a feature that is never legitimately zero inside the brain (`rms_lf`, say)
before computing any statistic over the volume, or the out-of-brain voxels will drag every
mean towards zero.
:::

## Ephys edges

An encoding volume says what the ephys signature is at each voxel. Its **edges** say
where that signature changes fastest — boundaries between electrophysiologically distinct
territories, found from the features alone.

The edges of the published vintages (`2026_W39` onwards) sit next to the volume on S3.
`download_edges_volume` takes the same arguments as `download_encoding_volume`:

```python
from ephysatlas.data import download_edges_volume

edges_file = download_edges_volume(local_path, label="2026_W42", one=one)
edges = np.load(edges_file)["ephys_atlas_vol"][..., 0]   # (ML, AP, DV) float16, 0 outside the mask
```

The file has the encoding volume's layout, so it reads the same way: a single feature,
`feature_names = ["ephys_edges"]`, 6 MB at 50 µm.

### Derive them yourself

To recompute the edges, or derive them with other settings:

```python
from ephysatlas.edges import compute_edges_volume

edges = compute_edges_volume(file_path)   # (AP, ML, DV) float32, NaN outside the mask
```

The volume is z-scored and rotated onto its principal components. The components that
explain 95 % of the variance are kept and whitened, so Euclidean distance between voxels
is their Mahalanobis distance in feature space; `2026_W42` keeps 7. Each component is
Gaussian-smoothed (σ = 100 µm, NaN-aware) and its gradient magnitude taken, per mm. The
magnitudes are then aggregated across components:

| `aggregate` | units |
|---|---|
| `"median"` (default) | median across PCs of the whitened PC gradient magnitude, per mm — robust to a PC that changes alone |
| `"mean"` | mean across PCs, per mm |

Voxels within 100 µm of the mask border are dropped (`erode_um`), because their gradient
is a mask artefact. `void` and `void_fluid` are excluded; `root` is kept, as it contains
fibre tracts. The mask comes from `iblatlas.atlas.AllenAtlas(res_um)` unless you pass
`atlas=`, and that atlas downloads its Allen volumes on first use.

`compute_edges_volume` also writes `brainwide_ephys_edges_{res_um}um.npz` next to the
volume (or to `out_file=`), in the layout published on S3:

| key | content |
|---|---|
| `ephys_atlas_vol` | `(ML, AP, DV, 1)` float16 edge strength, e.g. `(228, 264, 160, 1)` at 50 µm; 0 outside the eroded mask |
| `feature_names` | `["ephys_edges"]` |
| `res_um`, `grid_shape` | As in the encoding volume |
| `axis_order` | `"ML,AP,DV"` |
| `units` | The `aggregate`'s units, as in the table above |
| `aggregate`, `sigma_um`, `erode_um`, `n_pcs`, `variance_threshold`, `exclude_acronyms`, `source` | The settings used, for the record |

On the `2026_W42` volume this takes about 5 seconds and reproduces the published file
exactly; 61 % of the grid is outside the eroded brain mask (NaN), and the median edge
strength is 1.6 per mm.

For other settings, the steps are separate functions: `load_whitened_pcs` (whitened PCs
and the valid mask), `edge_strength` (smoothed gradient, aggregated) and
`save_edges_volume` (write in the encoding volume's layout). See the
[edges API](../api/edges.compute_edges_volume.qmd).
